# AlgaMatrix: A membrane-based microalgae photobioreactor for indoor bio-integrated systems

Benedetta Zuccarelli , Ziqi (Lydia) Yan, Yihan (Angelina) Zhang, Xinyi (Skye) Gao

and Daniel Tish

Architecture, Harvard University Graduate School of Design, Cambridge, USA

Abstract

Indoor environmental performance is commonly addressed through energy-intensive mechanical systems with limited integration into architectural components. Algae-based systems show potential for carbon uptake and environmental mediation, yet most applications focus on façade-scale or exhibition prototypes, with limited validation in interiors. This research develops AlgaMatrix, a modular interior photobioreactor conceived as an architectural component. The system cultivates Chlorella vulgaris within ultrasonically welded thermoplastic membranes supported by 3D-printed frames. Continuous fluid circulation and embedded sensing enable monitoring of biological activity and localized CO2 variation. Computational fluid dynamics simulations informed internal channel geometry and circulation strategies to promote uniform flow and reduce sedimentation, linking digital design to fabrication constraints. A 14-day comparative experiment demonstrated sustained biomass growth in the circulating system, while a static control declined. Localized CO2 reductions occurred during peak photosynthesis. The study establishes a reproducible framework for integrating and monitoring biological processes within fabricated architectural systems, advancing adaptive indoor ecologies.

Impact statement

AlgaMatrix proposes a modular, digitally fabricated microalgae photobioreactor that integrates living biological systems into interior architectural components, demonstrating sustained growth and localized CO2 reduction under ambient indoor conditions. By combining membrane fabrication, circulation logic, and real-time sensing, the project establishes a measurable and replicable framework for biologically informed interior environments.

Introduction

As climate change intensifies and urban environments become increasingly exposed to extreme heat, air pollution, and resource scarcity, the regulation of indoor environments has emerged as a critical architectural challenge. Contemporary life is increasingly interiorized: people in industrialized societies spend approximately 90% of their time indoors (Allen and Macomber, 2020; Satish et al., 2012), making indoor environmental quality central to human health and well-being. Since the mid-twentieth century, buildings have increasingly depended on mechanical systems to regulate indoor temperature and air quality. While these systems have enabled standardized comfort conditions, they also entail significant energy demand, generate waste heat and contribute to greenhouse gas emissions, thereby intensifying the climatic pressures they seek to mitigate. Architectural theory has long framed interior environments as artificially stabilized systems, insulated from external climatic variability through technological mediation. Banham’s Architecture of the Well-Tempered Environment (1984) describes this condition as one in which environmental performance is delegated to mechanical infrastructure rather than embedded within architectural form or material logic. In this framework, comfort is maintained through continuous mechanical buffering, allowing the architectural envelope to become increasingly indifferent to climate as long as energy supply remains uninterrupted. As climate instability increases, the separation between architecture and environmental regulation becomes increasingly untenable. This challenge calls for a reduction in energy demand alongside a reconceptualization of buildings as operative elements within environmental processes. Within this context, living materials have gained renewed attention as potential mediators between biological processes and architectural systems. Microalgae, among the earliest photosynthetic organisms, have played a foundational role in regulating Earth’s atmospheric composition. Their capacity to absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen through

photosynthesis positions them as promising agents for biologically integrated environmental regulation (Barsanti, 2022). Unlike ground-based plant systems, microalgae are cultivated within enclosed and controlled photobioreactor environments that can be directly integrated into building envelopes, enabling regulated growth conditions and optimized productivity for architectural applications (Arora et al., 2024; Razzak et al., 2024). Recent architectural research has explored algae-based systems primarily at the scale of façades or exhibition-oriented installations. While these projects demonstrate the conceptual potential of integrating living systems into architecture, they often rely on large infrastructural investments, complex maintenance regimes or lack systematic long-term performance validation under real-world conditions. There remains a lack of experimentally validated, small-scale systems designed specifically for indoor environments, where constraints of space, light, maintenance, and fabrication are more stringent. Addressing this gap requires a shift from symbolic or display-driven bio-integration toward fabrication-driven, performance-tested architectural systems. This paper presents AlgaMatrix, a digitally fabricated, modular microalgae photobioreactor designed for indoor architectural integration. The system cultivates Chlorella vulgaris within ultrasonically welded thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) membranes supported by 3D-printed structural frames, enabling controlled experimentation with biological performance and environmental interaction. This research contributes in three ways: (1) by developing a fabrication-driven framework for integrating living microalgae into modular architectural assemblies; (2) by evaluating microalgal growth and fluid behavior under indoor conditions through embedded sensing and Multiphysics simulation; and (3) by positioning bio-integrated systems as reproducible material infrastructures for adaptive interior environments.

State of the art

Microalgae integration in architecture has been explored through façades, modular systems, and bio-design prototypes that position buildings as hosts for metabolic processes. While these approaches demonstrate technical feasibility, challenges remain in scalability, fabrication complexity, user interaction, and long-term maintenance. The BIQ House in Hamburg exemplifies a large-scale bioreactor façade integrating biomass production, shading, and thermal regulation (Arup, 2013), though its infrastructural complexity limits broader replicability. EcoClosure (Kim, 2022) investigates photobioreactor glazing at the component scale through rigid panelized envelope systems. Other projects, such as the WaterLilly microalgae wall (Peters, 2014), deploy membrane assemblies as façade skins within exhibition contexts, using

continuous planar surfaces to contain algae cultures. More recent studies investigate 3D-printed façade-integrated algae modules combining tubular cultivation and air-driven circulation to interact with indoor air at the building envelope scale (Chen et al., 2025) (Figure 1). Within this body of work, fewer studies have explored interior-scale algae systems that combine bio-integration with sensing technologies, environmental monitoring, and user interaction at the room scale. Existing systems primarily focus on façade performance, energy exchange or biomass production, while questions related to algae viability, maintenance, and environmental responsiveness within everyday indoor environments remain less developed. Parallel research on indoor environmental sensing has demonstrated how accessible interfaces can translate invisible environmental conditions into intuitive feedback for occupants (Jo et al., 2020; Zuccarelli et al., 2025). Comparable approaches remain limited in bio-integrated architectural systems, particularly in relation to monitoring, environmental awareness, and user engagement. This direction is aligned with recent work in bio design and bio fabrication, where biological systems are increasingly framed as materially and environmentally interdependent assemblies in which geometry, fabrication, and biological activity are closely coupled (Andréen and Goidea, 2022; Armaly et al., 2023). In this context, AlgaMatrix is positioned as an alternative approach for hosting living microalgae within interior architectural space. The project investigates how inflatable membrane architectures can support algae viability, circulation, sensing, and user interaction through freestanding and modular interior components. Unlike façade-integrated photobioreactors embedded within the building envelope, the system operates independently from façade infrastructure under indoor environmental conditions. Positioned near natural light sources, it uses inflatable TPU membranes with continuous welded channels for fluid circulation. Existing algae systems commonly rely on rigid panels, glazing units, tubular reactors or continuous membrane surfaces. AlgaMatrix employs welded inflatable membrane assemblies, where internal flow paths are integrated directly within a continuous TPU volume. This strategy draws from bag-based cultivation methods used in aquaculture and translates them into architectural components designed for interior environments (Arora et al., 2024; Razzak et al., 2024). The project also integrates sensing technologies that monitor environmental and biological conditions while enabling forms of user feedback and interaction. Interior deployment introduces constraints related to lower light availability, closer user proximity, and accessible maintenance requirements. The system therefore relies on low-pressure circulation, compact modular assemblies, and embedded sensing strategies that support algae survival alongside environmental awareness. Within this framework, biological performance is closely linked to fabrication and interaction, where membrane

Methods

Biological constraints and material selection

Microalgal species selection The integration of microalgae into thin-film membrane systems imposes biological constraints related to growth rate, environmental tolerance, and compatibility with synthetic materials (Castro-Mu˜noz et al., 2021; Masojídek and Torzillo, 2008). To identify a species suitable for indoor membrane-based cultivation, a comparative study was conducted between two widely studied microalgae: Chlorella vulgaris and Dunaliella salina. Both species are recognized for their resilience and have been explored in bioregenerative life-support research in enclosed environments (Revellame et al., 2024). C. vulgaris is a freshwater microalga characterized by rapid growth, efficient nutrient uptake, and high photosynthetic activity, with extensive applications in environmental remediation and carbon sequestration studies (Masojídek and Torzillo, 2008). It also exhibits high nutritional value and significant carbon sequestration potential (Politaeva et al., 2023). In contrast, D. salina is a halophilic species adapted to high-salinity and environmentally stressful conditions. Both species were cultured using equivalent initial concentrations to evaluate comparative growth performance. During the preliminary screening phase, C. vulgaris and D. salina cultures were obtained from Algae Research Supply. C. vulgaris cultures and modified f/2 nutrient media were supplied through the manufacturer’s algae culture kit and maintenance formulations (Algae Research Supply, n.d.-a), advertised as a complete medium modified from the Guillard and Ryther f/2 formulation for freshwater and seawater algal cultures (Guillard, 1975), while D. salina was maintained using the supplier’s recommended seawater medium for halophilic microalgae (Algae Research Supply, n.d.-b). No formal strain identifiers or accession numbers were provided by the supplier. Due to limited access to wet-lab facilities, cultivation was conducted in a

semi-controlled indoor studio environment in Cambridge, MA, during April. Culture flasks were positioned near a west-facing window under mixed natural and artificial illumination, with supplemental lighting operating on a 16:8 h light/dark cycle. Ambient temperatures ranged between approximately 20–26°C. Light intensity and spectral composition were not quantitatively measured. Cultures were continuously agitated on a laboratory shaker at an estimated 100–110 rpm to maintain suspension, support gas exchange, and reduce sedimentation of C. vulgaris cells. Continuous mixing promotes circulation and improves light and nutrient distribution within the culture volume (Ahmad et al., 2024; Akhtar et al., 2020). The cultivation environment was intended as an early-stage assessment of biological compatibility and material integration within the AlgaMatrix membrane system rather than a fully standardized physiological growth study. Cultures were monitored over a ten-day period. Hemocytometer observations supported qualitative comparison of culture development; however, limitations in sampling homogeneity, starting cell density and biological replication constrained interpretation of cell counts as precise whole-culture density measurements. The study therefore focused primarily on culture viability, handling stability and suitability for membrane-based prototype cultivation (Figure 2).

Membrane material selection The membrane serves as the primary interface between biological processes and architectural fabrication, requiring a balance of optical clarity, mechanical flexibility, chemical stability, and longterm durability. The system demands a material capable of withstanding repeated inflation cycles, maintaining sealed fluid channels and supporting sustained biological activity without excessive biofouling. TPU was selected over bioplastics and other polymer alternatives due to its superior tensile strength, elasticity, and resistance to chemical degradation (Shin et al. 2025). Although TPU carries a higher embodied carbon than some biodegradable polymers, its extended lifespan and resistance to cracking and delamination reduce the frequency of replacement, mitigating environmental impact over the system’s operational life. TPU exhibits limited gas permeability. As passive diffusion through

Microalgae can operate under multiple metabolic modes, including photo-autotrophy (lightdriven growth), mixotrophy (combined light and organic carbon uptake), and heterotrophy (growth without light) (Verma et al., 2020). As photosynthetic activity depends on light availability, optical transmission was evaluated as a key parameter in the membrane system. Clear TPU allowed visible light transmission under indoor cultivation conditions. A material compatibility experiment was conducted to evaluate TPU–microalgae interactions under semi-controlled cultivation conditions. Membranes were tested using a full-factorial design combining three thicknesses (0.15, 0.3, and 0.5 mm) with three surface finishes (clear, opaque, and black). Different surface finishes were included to examine how variations in membrane optical properties and pigmentation affected cultivation behavior and surface interaction during the testing period. Cultures of C. vulgaris and D. salina were monitored over a seven-day period to evaluate optical transmission, surface-associated accumulation, condensation/ residue formation, and growth consistency across TPU material variants (Figure 3). semi-controlled indoor conditions. Comparative ratings (low, moderate, high) were used to support early-stage material selection and prototype evaluation.

Fabrication and computational design

Membrane fabrication AlgaMatrix membrane system is fabricated through CNC-controlled ultrasonic welding of dual-layer TPU sheets. An ultrasonic welding head mounted on a ZUND cutting platform generates localized heat through high-frequency vibration, fusing layers along predefined seams without adhesives, enabling precise control of geometry while preserving flexibility and optical clarity (Figure 4). Welding tests were conducted to optimize seam integrity, leak resistance, and transparency by maintaining a constant pressure of 4.5 bar while varying weld spacing from 0.5–4 mm and the number of welds passes from one to three. The welding process enabled the fabrication of internal channel geometries that define fluid routing and influence fluid circulation, with constraints such as minimum seam spacing and curvature radius informing the design. Multiple geometric configurations were iteratively tested to evaluate flow distribution, structural behavior, and scalability across modular assemblies (Figure 5). Fabrication accuracy was validated through prototype testing, while digital reference points informed seam

Computational design and flow simulation Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations are widely used to model flow behavior and inform the design of photobioreactor systems (Ahmad et al., 2024; Luzi and McHardy, 2022). In this study, CFD simulations informed membrane geometry and circulation strategy. Internal fluid dynamics were modeled in COMSOL Multiphysics usinga laminar flow interface, with an inflow velocity of 0.108 m/s derived from pump testing and applied consistently across scenarios. These simulations enabled early-stage evaluation of flow behavior prior to fabrication, reducing reliance on trial-and-error prototyping. Five geometric configurations (Prototypes A–E) were evaluated to compare pressure distribution, velocity profiles, and scalability under modular aggregation. All configurations were based on a tetrahedral unit, with variations in channel routing, inlet positioning, and aggregation logic. Both single modules and multilayered assemblies were simulated to assess interconnected flow behavior. Maintaining consistent flow distribution is essential for stable nutrient transport and gas exchange within membrane-based microalgae systems. Circulation influences the growth dynamics of C. vulgaris by regulating mass transfer within the culture medium, including nutrient diffusion, CO2 availability, and oxygen removal. In static conditions, boundary layers form at the membrane–fluid interface, limiting dissolved inorganic carbon transport and allowing localized oxygen supersaturation, which can inhibit photosynthetic efficiency (Becker, 1994; Torzillo and Vonshak, 2013).

Hydrodynamic mixing disrupts these gradients, enhancing gas– liquid exchange, and improving biomass productivity through more uniform carbon delivery and reduced sedimentation (Ugwu et al., 2008). In membrane-based photobioreactors with constrained flow paths, controlled circulation therefore supports a more consistent photosynthetic performance and biomass accumulation. At a methodological level, computational modeling functioned as a feedback mechanism linking hydraulic analysis, biological requirements, and fabrication strategy throughout the prototyping process. This approach aligns with recent discussions in biologically informed design and bio fabrication, which describe biological systems as materially and environmentally interdependent design environments where geometry, fabrication, and organism behavior are closely coupled (Andréen and Goidea, 2022; Armaly et al., 2023).

Prototype architecture

The AlgaMatrix prototype translates membrane-based cultivation into a modular architectural system capable of spatial deployment, continuous operation, and environmental monitoring. Structure, fluid circulation, sensing, and biological processes are integrated within a repeatable module (Figure 6). This section outlines the system’s architectural logic, focusing on modular geometry, structural components, joint design, and the integration of pumps and sensors for sustained operation.

Modular geometry and structural system

The fundamental architectural unit of AlgaMatrix is a tetrahedral module composed of a dual-layer TPU membrane supported by a rigid structural frame. The tetrahedral geometry was selected for its inherent structural stability, spatial efficiency, and ability to aggregate into larger assemblies without requiring additional secondary support. When combined, individual tetrahedral units form hexagonal patterns that enhance structural cohesion while enabling flexible and freestanding installations. The structural frame is fabricated through additive manufacturing using polylactic acid (PLA), a biodegradable thermoplastic chosen for its balance between mechanical strength, dimensional stability, and environmental responsibility. Frames are produced in two interlocking sizes, with hollow interiors designed to accommodate tubing for microalgae circulation, effectively integrating structure, and infrastructure within a single component. Additive manufacturing further enables rapid iteration and customization of module dimensions, supporting adaptation to different spatial conditions and scales through low-setup and highly customizable fabrication processes.

Joint design and fluid connectivity

At the interface between membrane and structure, AlgaMatrix employs snap-fit joints that regulate fluid flow, enable modular connectivity, and ensure watertight integration (Figure 7).

The joints are fabricated using a high-resolution PolyJet 3D printing process on a Stratasys J55 platform, utilizing VeroClear resin for its transparency, chemical stability, and dimensional precision. Each joint is designed with a standardized 20 mm base that anchors it to the PLA structural frame, while the opposing end accommodates inlets, outlets, air filters or tubing connections. The transparency of the joints was intended to support visual inspection of flow behavior at critical connection points during operation. Joints can be replaced or reconfigured without damaging the membrane or structural frame, allowing the system to adapt to different algae strains, flow rates or experimental setups. Air filters are embedded directly into the membrane at designated locations to enable gas exchange while preserving a sealed liquid environment. The filter housings were customdesigned and fabricated via 3D printing (Ø 20 mm) to integrate with the membrane joints. A gas-permeable film was inserted between two transparent 3D-printed joint components, forming a sealed interface that allows CO2 and O2 transfer while preventing liquid leakage. During fabrication, extended membrane edges were left unsealed to allow insertion of the filter assembly, after which the edges were cut and re-welded to restore watertight integrity.

Pumping system and circulation logic

Continuous fluid circulation is a core operational requirement of the AlgaMatrix system, supporting nutrient distribution, preventing biomass sedimentation, and enhancing photosynthetic efficiency (Akhtar et al., 2020; Razzak et al., 2024). Circulation is achieved through low-voltage water pumps connected to the membrane modules via integrated tubing housed within the structural frames. Pump selection and calibration were informed by early testing to establish flow rates compatible with both biological viability and membrane durability. Circulation was driven by a pump calibrated to deliver an average internal flow velocity of approximately 0.108 m/s, consistent with values used in computational simulation. This velocity was selected to maintain nutrient distribution and minimize sedimentation while limiting internal pressure to levels compatible with membrane seam integrity.

Sensor integration and monitoring infrastructure

AlgaMatrix integrates embedded sensors within an Internet of Things (IoT) framework to evaluate biological performance and environmental interaction. This monitoring system supports both experimental analysis and future user interaction with bio-

The prototype incorporates total dissolved solids (TDS) sensors to track microalgae growth (Biechele et al., 2015; Rostam et al., 2021) and CO2 sensors positioned near the membrane to detect localized concentration changes. Data is collected via microcontrollers and transmitted wirelessly using the Message Queuing Telemetry Transport protocols to a centralized cloud platform, enabling continuous logging and remote access to performance metrics (Figure 8). A mobile interface allows users to visualize real-time data, track trends over time, and adjust system parameters such as pump intervals. By externalizing system intelligence through a digital interface, AlgaMatrix extends architectural agency beyond static material form, allowing occupants to engage with biological processes as part of the built environment. Sensor integration also enables the identification of system limitations, including flow irregularities and sensor drift, informing iterative refinement of both fabrication and operation.

Experimental setup

Biological viability and environmental interactions of the AlgaMatrix system are assessed through a controlled in-situ experiment comparing microalgae growth within the fabricated membrane to a static control culture. The evaluation focused on two primary performance indicators: biomass accumulation, measured through TDS and localized carbon dioxide variation in the immediate vicinity of the membrane-integrated air filters. The prototype was positioned approximately 25 cm from a west-facing window in Cambridge, MA, under natural daylight conditions in April, resulting in direct afternoon sunlight exposure (Figure 9). The experimental protocol consisted of two identical cultures of C. vulgaris prepared using the same growth medium, initial concentration and incubation conditions (Table 1). One culture served as a static control and was maintained in a conventional 600 mL laboratory vessel equipped with a gas-permeable membrane. The

second culture was circulated continuously through a fully assembled AlgaMatrix membrane module. Both systems were placed within the same indoor environment under ambient light and stable temperature conditions throughout the testing period. The AlgaMatrix module was connected to an external incubation reservoir via integrated tubing and operated with a programmable pump calibrated to maintain consistent flow velocity. Circulation was set to ensure continuous nutrient exchange while avoiding excessive mechanical stress on the membrane. Biological growth was monitored over a 14-day period to demonstrate the system’s feasibility and functionality. TDS sensors were deployed to record changes in dissolved solids as a proxy for biomass accumulation, while CO2 sensors were positioned near the membrane-integrated air filter to capture localized variations in carbon dioxide concentration. Measurements were conducted in an occupied indoor room during the spring season in Cambridge, MA, with the building’s heating, ventilation, and air conditioning system operating under typical conditions. Ventilation rates and occupancy were not experimentally controlled. Sensor data were logged continuously via the IoT infrastructure (Figure 10).

Results

Material and fabrication performance

Over the ten-day observation period, C. vulgaris demonstrated more robust visible culture development than D. salina under the semi-controlled indoor cultivation conditions used in this study. Hemocytometer observations supported a qualitative comparison of culture behavior and provided approximate cell-density estimates. Fabrication performance Fabrication testing demonstrated that ultrasonic welding parameters significantly influenced membrane integrity, inflation behavior, and circulation stability. Variations in welding pressure, seam spacing, and weld repetition produced observable differences in leakage resistance and membrane deformation during inflation and fluid circulation tests. The most reliable welding configuration consisted of a double weld executed at 4.5 bar pressure with a 4 mm seam spacing. Single welds frequently produced seam discontinuities and localized leakage, while seam spacing below 3 mm resulted in weld overlap and thermal deformation due to localized overheating. Similarly, a single weld pass generated weaker seams, whereas three passes caused partial melting and material distortion. A configuration of two weld passes provides the best balance between seal integrity and material stability. The selected 0.3 mm TPU membrane maintained structural stability across repeated inflation cycles without rupture or significant deformation, supporting consistent circulation performance and repeatable assembly behavior (Table 3). These fabrication optimizations directly informed the integration of the membrane system with the structural and hydraulic assembly. Embedding fluid routing within the frame minimized external tubing exposure and supported a more cohesive architectural assembly. The snap-fit joint system further enabled repeated assembly, disassembly, and module replacement during experimental iterations without damaging the membrane structure. Flow simulation and circulation behavior

Results showed clear differences in hydraulic performance across the tested configurations. Among the five evaluated geometries (Figure 13), Prototypes B and C exhibited stronger pressure accumulation near inlet regions and pronounced localized velocity gradients at module junctions, indicating increased risk of uneven nutrient transport and stagnation under multi-module deployment. Prototype E demonstrated improved flow continuity relative to B, C, and D but retained localized pressure concentrations near peripheral branches. Prototype A showed the most balanced circulation behavior, with more distributed flow pathways and reduced pressure concentration across interconnected modules

and was therefore selected for fabrication and subsequent sensing experiments. Although localized low-velocity regions remained present near peripheral nodes, these areas were spatially limited and did not produce complete flow interruption during circulation testing. The CFD analysis identified localized low-velocity regions and potential hydraulic dead zones within portions of the membrane geometry. The simulations served as an exploratory designguiding tool for comparing flow behavior across prototype configurations and identifying circulation constraints within the system. Internal flow simulations were conducted using an average inlet velocity of approximately 0.108 m/s derived from pump testing. The membrane system operated with an approximate internal fluid volume of 600mL. Residence time distribution and flow turnover were not experimentally characterized in this earlystage prototype study. Alternative inlet configurations, including bottom-fed up-flow circulation strategies, may reduce stagnation regions and will be investigated in future iterations. Simulation outputs of Prototype A were compared with physical circulation experiments and showed general agreement with observed flow behavior, with deviations primarily associated with membrane deformation under pressure. Circulation testing confirmed continuous fluid propagation across interconnected membrane channels within the fabricated assembly. Biomass growth results (TDS) and local environmental measurements

TDS measurements revealed distinct growth trajectories between the static control culture and the AlgaMatrix system. During approximately the first 2–2.5 days of the experiment, both cultures exhibited a similar decline in TDS values, consistent with an acclimation phase commonly observed when microalgae are transferred to new cultivation environments. Following this initial period, the two systems diverged. The static control showed a gradual decline or stabilization in TDS levels, indicating limited biomass accumulation and reduced nutrient exchange typical of non-circulating systems. In contrast, the AlgaMatrix culture

demonstrated a sustained increase in TDS values beginning at approximately Day 2.5, as indicated by both the raw measurements and the moving average (MA) trend (Figure 14). Quantitatively, the AlgaMatrix culture increased from a post-acclimation baseline of approximately 750 ppm (Day 2.5) to peak values exceeding 1,000 ppm between Days 8–11, corresponding to a net gain of approximately 250–300 ppm (33-40%). On the other hand, the static control exhibited a slight net decrease of approximately 6–13%. This separation in TDS trajectories emerged during the mid-experiment phase, with AlgaMatrix TDS consistently exceeding the control from Days 5–11, indicating sustained biomass growth under circulating conditions. The AlgaMatrix prototype exhibited regular diurnal fluctuations in TDS measurements, with cyclical increases and decreases broadly aligned with daily light exposure patterns. These oscillations suggest photosynthetic activity, biomass turnover, and dynamic dissolved solids behavior under circulating conditions. While the photobioreactor (PBR) supported sustained microalgal activity, it did not consistently exceed the static culture across the full test period; by Day 14, the static culture reached higher biomass proxy values. These results indicate that system performance is sensitive to batch conditions and resource availability, rather than demonstrating a

Discussion

This study examines a membrane-based microalgae system at the interior scale, where biological performance is shaped by the interaction between geometry, membrane fabrication, and fluid circulation. The results demonstrate that the AlgaMatrix system can sustain biological activity under ambient indoor conditions while maintaining stable circulation within a fabricated membrane assembly. A central outcome of the study is the role of fabrication precision in governing hydraulic and biological behavior. Ultrasonically welded TPU membranes enabled the formation of sealed circulation channels, while welding tolerances, seam spacing, and inlet positioning directly influenced flow continuity, pressure distribution, and membrane stability. Earlier prototypes exhibited leakage, localized stagnation, and uneven inflation behavior, demonstrating how small fabrication inconsistencies can propagate into larger operational effects. Iterative refinements to seam geometry and circulation routing improved hydraulic stability across inflated and aggregated modules, positioning welding logic as both a structural and circulation-defining mechanism within the system. The circulating AlgaMatrix cultures achieved a 33–40% increase in biomass concentration, while the static control declined over the same period. Temporal fluctuations in TDS measurements reflected continued responsiveness to daylight cycles, indicating sustained photosynthetic activity under interior conditions. At the same time, the transition toward a resource-

limited phase near the end of the testing period highlights constraints inherent to batch cultivation and underscores the importance of longer operational studies for evaluating sustained productivity, material durability, and biofouling behavior. Localized CO2 reductions of 20–40 ppm near the membrane-filter interface further indicate that environmental effects remain spatially confined. These findings suggest that systems such as AlgaMatrix operate most effectively as distributed architectural elements integrated within proximity-based conditions, including partitions, interior surfaces or window-adjacent assemblies. In this context, the membrane functions as an active environmental interface that spatially links occupants, airflow, and biological processes at the local scale. More broadly, the study positions membrane-based cultivation systems as fabrication-driven architectural assemblies in which biological growth, circulation behavior, sensing, and material organization are closely coupled. By integrating computational simulation, ultrasonic welding, environmental sensing and living microalgae within a modular bag-based system, the project establishes a framework for evaluating bio-integrated architectural components under realistic indoor conditions.

Limitations and next steps

This study presents a prototype-scale implementation of a microalgae-integrated architectural membrane system. The findings are specific to the current experimental configuration and should be interpreted within the scope of this prototype-scale study. Biological growth was monitored over a 14-day period under controlled indoor conditions, demonstrating sustained microalgal activity and stable circulation behavior. This timeframe establishes initial feasibility and system functionality, but does not capture long-term performance, membrane durability or maintenance requirements. Extended operational testing is necessary to evaluate material stability, biofouling, and sustained biological activity over time. The observed environmental effects remained localized. Variations in CO2 concentration occurred near the air filter region and did not influence room-scale air quality. Accordingly, the system should not be interpreted as a replacement for mechanical ventilation. Its contribution lies in providing a framework for embedding biological processes within architectural assemblies and enabling localized environmental interaction. Conclusion

This study demonstrates the feasibility of integrating microalgae cultivation within membrane-based architectural systems at the interior scale. The AlgaMatrix prototype combines membrane fabrication, hydraulic circulation, sensing, and biological activity within a single architectural assembly, where performance is shaped by the relationship between geometry, welding logic, and fluid flow. Fabrication testing showed that welding parameters directly influenced membrane integrity and circulation behavior. The most reliable configuration consisted of a double weld at 4.5 bar with 4 mm seam spacing and two welding passes, which reduced leakage, and improved seam continuity during inflation and circulation tests. Seam spacing below 3 mm caused weld overlap and localized overheating, while single-pass welds produced weaker seam integrity. Iterative refinements to seam geometry, inlet positioning, and channel continuity reduced stagnation zones and improved pressure distribution across inflated membrane modules. Computational fluid simulations guided geometric refinement prior to fabrication, while physical testing verified circulation stability during operation and module aggregation. Circulating cultures achieved a 33–40% increase in biomass concentration (250–300 ppm TDS), while the static control declined by 6–13% over the same period. Temporal variation in TDS measurements reflected continued photosynthetic response to daylight exposure, while localized CO2 reductions of 20–40 ppm near the membrane-filter interface indicated spatially confined environmental effects. Although evaluated within a limited experimental timeframe, the study demonstrates that membrane-based cultivation systems can be spatially deployed, hydraulically stabilized, and empirically monitored within interior environments. The contribution of this work lies in establishing a fabrication-driven framework for bagbased microalgae cultivation in which ultrasonic welding defines both structural continuity and internal circulation behavior, integrating digital simulation, membrane fabrication, sensing, and biological growth within a cohesive architectural system.
